newsitem.title: FINLAND: FINNISH PM SEES SUCCESS IN EMU FOR FOREST INDUSTRY.
newsitem.headline: FINNISH PM SEES SUCCESS IN EMU FOR FOREST INDUSTRY.

text.p: Prime Minister Paavo Lipponen said on Tuesday he expected Finnish forest industry companies to be successful also in a coming single currency environment.
"I have all reason to believe that the Finnish forest industry will enjoy continued success also inside economic and monetary union," Lipponen told a seminar in Skelleftea, Sweden.
A copy of his prepared speech was made available to the media in Helsinki.
Already now, before the transfer to the single currency, the euro, "the time is definitely behind when we could secure our competitiveness through exchange rate changes," he said.
Lipponen said the Finnish mechanical forest industry should raise the degree of refinement. That could also boost employment.

"The paper industry has already earlier successfully raised its degree of refinement. Now it is up to the mechanical side, the construction sector and the chemical industry to develop the possibilities of wood," he said.
According to a recent study Finland should be able to increase employment in the entire forestry sector by up to 65,000 people from the current 147,000, he said.
"This should be a joint target for the industry, for the trade unions and for the state," Lipponen said.
Together, Finnish and Swedish forest industry companies account for nearly two thirds of pulp output and over 40 percent of paper production in the European Union.
"In forestry issues we are not any small member countries," Lipponen said, adding the EU's forestry areas had doubled when Sweden, Finland and Austria joined in 1995.
In Finland's view, the EU needs a forest strategy, but not a common forestry policy like the Common Agricultural Policy, he said.
The goal of a forestry strategy should be to safeguard the European forestry sector's competitiveness on the increasingly global markets, Lipponen said, adding this was key to more jobs.
In EMU, the euro will fluctuate against the U.S. dollar -- an important currency for the forest industry, Lipponen said.
But it was a myth that the economies of Finland and Sweden would be more sensitive to fluctuations in the dollar than other European countries and more vulnerable in the single currency.
"The forest industry is depending on the dollar ... but the dependence on the euro will be strong from the beginning and will increase as time goes by," Lipponen said.
